case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal “Election Day” statutes preempt Mississippi’s law allowing absentee ballots to be received and counted up to five business days after Election Day in federal general elections.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. I, § 4 (Elections Clause) and art. II, § 1, cl. 4 (Presidential Electors Clause); federal Election Day statutes (e.g., 2 U.S.C. §§ 1 & 7 setting the “time” for choosing Representatives and Electors); and Mississippi’s receipt-deadline statute, Miss. Code Ann. § 23-15-637(1)(a).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Mississippi (Secretary of State Watson) argues that its five-business-day post–Election Day receipt deadline for absentee ballots does not conflict with, and therefore is not preempted by, the federal Election Day statutes or the Electors Clause. In its view, federal law fixes only the day on which voting begins or the general electoral event occurs, while States retain authority to administer the mechanics of casting, receiving, verifying, and counting ballots—processes that often necessarily continue after Election Day. Petitioner further contends the Fifth Circuit misread Supreme Court and circuit precedent (including Foster and cases like Bomer and Millsaps), and that it is implausible Congress intended Election Day statutes to impede citizens’ ability to vote—especially given later federal enactments like UOCAVA that reflect congressional solicitude for timely counting of certain absentee ballots. Petitioner emphasizes the high practical stakes and the need for immediate resolution to avoid election-administration chaos in close races.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Republican National Committee and aligned respondents argue the Fifth Circuit correctly held Mississippi’s receipt deadline is preempted because federal law requires the ‘choice’ of federal officers (including presidential electors) to occur on a single, nationally uniform Election Day, and allowing ballots to arrive and be counted after that day means the election is still ongoing and not ‘consummated.’ They maintain that while States can conduct post-election tabulation and verification, they cannot extend the period during which legally effective votes may be cast (via ballot receipt) beyond Election Day for federal general elections. Respondents also argue petitioner’s reliance on various precedents is misplaced because cases like Newberry did not address post–Election Day ballot receipt and RNC v. DNC involved a primary election (to which federal Election Day statutes do not apply). In their view, Supreme Court precedent (especially Foster) supports preemption here, and no controlling Supreme Court decision authorizes post–Election Day ballot receipt in general federal elections.
key_precedents: Republican National Committee v. Democratic National Committee, 589 U.S. 423 (2020) (per curiam)
Voting Integrity Project, Inc. v. Bomer, 199 F.3d 773 (5th Cir. 2000)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that a postmark by Election Day captures the voter’s completed “act of choice,” and she reads later receipt as merely administrative in the way canvassing is. But as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Thomas emphasize, Mississippi’s rule does not treat the vote as legally operative upon that Election Day act; it conditions legal effectiveness on a post–Election Day event (receipt), which—unlike tabulation—determines whether the ballot may lawfully enter the count at all, extending the legally operative period beyond the single day Congress fixed. Foster v. Love is not confined to “early election” schemes; its core instruction is that Congress fixed a uniform day on which the election must be legally consummated, and a receipt window creates a state-specific extension of when decisive votes can become valid inputs. Justice Sotomayor’s statutory-silence and disenfranchisement concerns are serious, but under a minimalist, precedent-respecting approach I cannot infer from silence a general authorization to count ballots that become legally effective after Election Day, particularly where (as Justice Gorsuch notes) Congress has enacted explicit, targeted exceptions like UOCAVA.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest contention—that a postmark by Election Day captures the voter’s legally relevant “act of choice,” with later receipt merely administrative—fails under the text Congress enacted and Foster v. Love’s instruction that the federally prescribed “time” requires the election to be legally consummated on that day. Mississippi’s rule does not treat the vote as legally operative when cast; it makes legal effectiveness contingent on a post–Election Day event (receipt), thereby extending the period during which new, outcome-determinative votes may lawfully enter the count, which is different in kind from post-day canvassing or tabulation. Justice Gorsuch’s point about UOCAVA reinforces the proper inference for a textualist: when Congress intends exceptions to the one-day rule, it speaks clearly, and we should not manufacture a general late-receipt authorization from statutory silence. Disenfranchisement concerns are serious, but as the Chief Justice notes they are policy matters for Congress, not a basis to revise §§ 1 and 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that the voter’s “act of choice” is complete by Election Day when the ballot is postmarked, making later receipt merely administrative; but that reframing cannot overcome Foster v. Love’s focus on when the election is legally consummated—i.e., when a vote becomes legally effective for the State’s final selection. As the Chief Justice notes, Mississippi’s rule makes legal effectiveness contingent on a post–Election Day event (receipt), so outcome-determinative votes may lawfully enter the count after the federal day Congress fixed, which is more than post-day canvassing or tabulation. Justice Sotomayor’s disenfranchisement concerns are serious as a matter of policy, but under the separation of powers and the textual structure—reinforced by Justice Gorsuch’s point about Congress’s express exceptions like UOCAVA—I do not read statutory silence in §§ 1 and 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1 as authorizing state-specific extensions of the federal election day. The narrowest sound holding is conflict preemption for federal offices where state law makes ballots countable only upon post–Election Day receipt, while leaving ample room for post-day verification and counting of timely received ballots.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is that Foster v. Love speaks of a single national day when the election must be "consummated," and they argue Mississippi extends the legally operative window because receipt occurs later. But Foster condemned a system where the election was effectively decided outside the federal day “with no act in law or in fact” on that day; Mississippi still anchors the legally relevant voter act—timely casting as evidenced by an Election-Day postmark—on the congressionally set day, with later receipt functioning like the post-day canvassing and tabulation Foster itself contemplated. Justice Gorsuch’s UOCAVA negative-implication argument does not supply the missing text: Congress’s creation of specific accommodations for distinct populations does not clearly federalize a universal receipt-by-midnight rule in §§ 1 and 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1, and I will not infer disenfranchising preemption from silence. Under my pragmatic, access-to-justice approach, the respondents’ uniformity concerns are real, but they cannot justify converting “time of choosing” into a physical-custody requirement that predictably penalizes voters who complied with Election Day but are thwarted by mail delays beyond their control.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s strongest point is that Foster v. Love speaks of a single national day on which the election must be “consummated,” and he reads Mississippi’s receipt rule as extending the legally operative period. But under a pragmatic textualist lens, “time of choosing” in §§ 1, 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1 is best tied to the voter’s legally required act (timely casting, evidenced here by an Election-Day postmark), while later receipt functions like other post-day mechanics (canvass, verification) that do not change when the choice is made. Justice Gorsuch’s UOCAVA negative-implication argument highlights that Congress can create explicit exceptions, yet it does not supply the missing affirmative text that converts “time” into a federal physical-custody/receipt-by-midnight mandate for all absentee ballots; reading that in risks statutory incoherence given Congress’s tolerance of post–Election Day counting in other contexts. Because the claimed conflict depends on importing a bright-line receipt deadline not in the federal statutes, I do not see direct conflict preemption on this record absent a clearer congressional command.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best point is that a timely postmark captures the voter’s act of choice on Election Day and treats later receipt as administration, but that re-describes—rather than answers—what the federal statutes fix: the “time” when votes may become legally operative in choosing federal officers. As the Chief Justice notes, Mississippi’s scheme makes a ballot legally effective only upon a post–Election Day event (receipt), so outcome-determinative votes can lawfully enter the count after the single day Congress prescribed, which is the conflict Foster v. Love identifies when it speaks of elections being “consummated” on the federal day. Justice Sotomayor’s appeal to statutory silence and disenfranchisement concerns cannot overcome the textual and structural inference reinforced by UOCAVA-type enactments: when Congress wants to allow counting ballots received after Election Day, it does so expressly rather than by implication. Under a separation-of-powers approach, the remedy for mail-delay hardships lies with Congress, not a judicially invented receipt exception to §§ 1 and 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that a timely postmark captures the voter’s act of choice on Election Day, with later receipt akin to post-day canvassing. But as the Chief Justice stresses, Mississippi does not treat the vote as legally operative upon that Election-Day act; it makes legal effectiveness contingent on a post–Election Day event (receipt), which in a close federal election extends the outcome-determinative window beyond the single day Congress fixed. Foster v. Love is not confined to “early election” schemes; its core instruction is about when the federal election is legally consummated, and a receipt window alters that consummation date rather than merely regulating administrative processing. Justice Gorsuch’s UOCAVA point reinforces my institutionalist approach: when Congress wants to permit post–Election Day counting in federal elections, it speaks clearly, and I am not prepared to infer a broad late-receipt authorization from the silence of §§ 1 and 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point—that the voter’s legally relevant act is complete on Election Day via a timely postmark, with later receipt merely administrative—has intuitive force, but it depends on treating “choice” as the voter’s subjective act rather than the State’s legal incorporation of that act into the binding tally. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, Foster’s concern is the federally fixed day on which the election is legally “consummated,” and Mississippi’s rule makes that consummation contingent on a post–Election Day event (receipt), not merely post-day canvassing or tabulation. Justice Gorsuch’s UOCAVA point reinforces this structurally: Congress has crafted explicit, targeted deviations from the one-day rule, which counsels against inferring a broad, silent authorization for post–Election Day receipt in general federal elections. Under a textualist/originalist approach attentive to precedent, I would keep the holding narrow but conclude the state receipt window conflicts with the federal command fixing a single day for the legally operative choice.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s strongest contention—that Foster v. Love requires legal “consummation” on Election Day and that Mississippi impermissibly extends the legally operative period because receipt occurs later—still does not persuade me because it treats “receipt” as the voter’s act of choosing rather than an administrative prerequisite to counting. Foster confronted a regime that effectively conducted and completed the choice outside the federal day “with no act in law or in fact” on Election Day; Mississippi, by contrast, anchors the voter’s legally required conduct to Election Day via postmark and simply recognizes that custody, verification, and tabulation necessarily happen later. Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Barrett’s negative-implication reliance on UOCAVA is a serious structural point, but it cannot supply a receipt-by-election-day rule that Congress did not write into §§ 1, 7, or 3 U.S.C. § 1, and I decline to find conflict preemption in silence where the practical consequence is disenfranchising voters who complied with the federal day’s command. On my procedural-fairness and consequences-aware approach, uniformity concerns cannot justify converting “time of choosing” into a federal physical-possession deadline untethered from statutory text.

John Roberts.reasoning: Congress, exercising its Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause authority, set a single, nationally uniform “time” for choosing Representatives and Electors on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November. 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7; 3 U.S.C. § 1. Under Foster v. Love, those statutes require that the federal election be “consummated” on Election Day, and a state may not extend the period during which legally effective votes may be cast beyond that day, even though tabulation and verification can occur afterward. Mississippi’s rule that treats ballots received up to five business days after Election Day as valid votes for federal offices conflicts with that federal command and is therefore preempted under the Supremacy Clause, and a narrow ruling limited to federal general elections best preserves uniformity and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause expressly authorize Congress to determine the “Time” of choosing Representatives and Electors, and Congress has done so by fixing a single, nationally uniform Election Day in 2 U.S.C. § 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1. Under the original public meaning reflected in this Court’s precedents, an “election” is the “final choice” of an officer by the electors, and federal law requires that choice to be “concluded” on Election Day, not extended by state law beyond it. Foster v. Love held that state schemes cannot “consummate” the choice on a day other than the congressionally prescribed day; allowing ballots to become legally effective upon receipt after Election Day similarly extends the time of choosing and conflicts with the federal statutes. While States retain broad authority over the “manner” of elections, post-election tabulation and verification are distinct from extending the period in which votes may be validly cast/received for federal offices, and the latter is preempted by Congress’s time-setting statutes.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. §§ 1 & 7) set the “time” for choosing Representatives and presidential electors as a single, nationally uniform day, and under the Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause that federal determination is controlling over contrary state rules. In Foster v. Love, 522 U.S. 67 (1997), the Court read those statutes to require that the election be “consummated” on the federally fixed day; Mississippi’s rule treating ballots not yet received by election officials until up to five business days later as legally effective votes extends the period of choice beyond that day. While States may canvass, verify, and tabulate after Election Day, permitting decisive votes to enter official custody after the day Congress chose undermines the bright-line administrability and uniformity Congress mandated and invites practical problems in close contests. Mississippi’s policy arguments and later enactments like UOCAVA cannot override the plain statutory timing rule absent a clear congressional authorization to accept and count ballots received after Election Day in federal general elections.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7; 3 U.S.C. § 1), enacted pursuant to the Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause, set a uniform day for the national electoral event, but they do not unmistakably require that every administrative condition for counting a timely-cast ballot—especially the State’s receipt and verification of mailed absentee ballots—be completed by midnight on Election Day. Foster v. Love held that a State may not “consummate” the election before Election Day, but it also recognized that aspects of the electoral process necessarily occur before and after that day; a modest post–Election Day receipt window for ballots cast by Election Day can fit comfortably within that understanding without extending voting beyond Election Day. Given Congress’s evident awareness of absentee voting and its later enactments protecting certain absentee voters (e.g., UOCAVA), I would not read the Election Day statutes to preempt Mississippi’s five-business-day receipt rule absent clearer congressional direction, particularly where the practical effect of preemption would be to disenfranchise voters who timely mailed ballots but are disadvantaged by mail delays. Construing federal law to preserve States’ traditional authority over election mechanics here best accords with the Constitution’s state-centered structure for administering elections and avoids needless harm to access to the ballot for vulnerable populations.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes set the "time" of choosing Representatives and Electors (2 U.S.C. §§ 1 & 7; 3 U.S.C. § 1), but they do not expressly require that every ballot be in officials’ hands by the end of that day, and Mississippi’s rule still requires the voter’s act of choice to be completed by Election Day via an Election-Day postmark. Foster v. Love preempted a scheme that "consummat[ed]" the election before the federal day "with no act in law or in fact" occurring on that day, 522 U.S. 67, 72 (1997); here, the legally effective act occurs on the federal day and what follows is receipt/canvass, a familiar administrative step. Reading the statutes to bar modest, administratively workable receipt windows would create serious practical disruption and sits uneasily with Congress’s later solicitude for absentee voting in statutes like UOCAVA, which presuppose that ballot handling and counting can extend beyond Election Day without altering the "day" of the election. On this text and precedent, I would not find conflict preemption merely because the State counts timely-cast absentee ballots received shortly after Election Day.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes set the "time" for choosing Representatives, Senators, and presidential electors as a single, nationally uniform day. 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7; 3 U.S.C. § 1. Under Foster v. Love, those statutes require that the State’s final, legally effective "choice" be "consummated" on that day, even though ministerial steps like tabulation and verification may occur afterward. 522 U.S. 67, 71–72 & n.4 (1997). Mississippi’s rule makes the legal effectiveness of an absentee ballot turn on receipt up to five business days after Election Day, thereby extending the period during which votes may be cast and counted for the federal election beyond the day Congress fixed, creating a conflict that is preempted under the Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause framework.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause, Congress may “determine the Time” of choosing Representatives and electors, and it has done so by fixing a single, nationally uniform Election Day in 2 U.S.C. §§ 1 & 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1. In Foster v. Love, this Court read those statutes to require that the legally effective “choice” occur on that day, and a state rule that makes a ballot legally effective only upon receipt after Election Day extends the time for the “choice” beyond the federally set day. Mississippi remains free to conduct post-election canvassing, verification, and tabulation after Election Day, but allowing additional legally countable ballots to be received and counted in the ensuing days conflicts with Congress’s one-day time rule and is therefore preempted. Practical workability and uniformity concerns reinforce that conclusion, particularly in close federal contests where varying state receipt windows would undermine the national Election Day framework.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes set the “time” for choosing Representatives and presidential electors, 2 U.S.C. §§ 1 & 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1, and those provisions are best read to require a single national deadline by which votes become legally effective in federal general elections. In Foster v. Love, 522 U.S. 67 (1997), the Court held States may not structure their rules so that the federal election is “consummated” on a day other than the congressionally designated Election Day, even while acknowledging that administrative steps like tabulation may occur afterward. Mississippi’s rule makes ballots legally effective upon receipt up to five business days after Election Day, thereby extending the period of legally effective voting beyond the federally fixed “time” for choosing federal officers. Under the Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause, state regulations yield to valid congressional timing rules, so Mississippi’s post–Election Day receipt deadline is preempted.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7; 3 U.S.C. § 1) set a uniform date for the federal general election, but they do not expressly regulate ballot-receipt deadlines or mandate that all ballots be in election officials’ possession by the close of polls on that date. Foster v. Love holds that the "election" must be "consummated" on Election Day, but Mississippi’s rule can be understood to consummate the voter’s choice on Election Day where the voter timely casts the ballot by that day and the State merely completes the receipt, verification, and tabulation that necessarily occur afterward. Given the Elections Clause’s allocation of primary administrative authority to the States subject to clear congressional override, I do not read these time-setting statutes to preempt a modest, nondiscriminatory receipt window that primarily promotes procedural fairness and avoids disenfranchisement from mail delays. Absent clearer congressional direction, preemption here would risk substantial practical harms to eligible voters without a correspondingly definite statutory command.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal law setting a single, uniform ‘Election Day’ for federal offices preempts Mississippi’s statute allowing absentee ballots to be received and counted up to five business days after Election Day.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Election Day statutes (setting the day for choosing presidential electors and Members of Congress) and the U.S. Constitution’s Electors Clause and Elections Clause, as applied to Mississippi’s ballot-receipt deadline (Miss. Code Ann. § 23-15-637(1)(a)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Mississippi (via its Secretary of State) argues that its rule permitting receipt and counting of timely-cast absentee ballots for several days after Election Day does not conflict with the federal Election Day statutes or the Electors/Elections Clauses, because the state can treat ballots as ‘cast’ by Election Day even if administratively received and processed afterward; petitioner emphasizes statutory text and historical practice, argues the Fifth Circuit misread precedent (especially Foster), and warns that the decision below has high-stakes, disruptive ramifications for election administration and close races.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The RNC and other Republican respondents argue that the federal Election Day statutes require final selection/choice to occur on the federally prescribed day for federal elections, and a state rule that keeps acceptance of ballots open after that day impermissibly extends the election period; they contend Mississippi’s post–Election Day receipt deadline means the election is not ‘consummated’ on Election Day and is therefore preempted under the Supremacy Clause, and they defend the Fifth Circuit’s application of Foster while distinguishing cases involving primaries or different contexts.
key_precedents: Republican National Committee v. Democratic National Committee (2020)
Voting Integrity Project, Inc. v. Bomer (5th Cir. 2000)
Voting Integrity Project, Inc. v. Keisling (9th Cir. 2001)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas present the strongest contrary argument: that Foster v. Love’s statement that the election is “consummated” on Election Day means the set of legally countable ballots must be closed that day, and Mississippi’s receipt rule keeps validity contingent on post-day events. But Foster’s holding addressed a State scheme that made the federal choice legally final before the congressionally fixed day; extending its “consummation” language to bar a fixed, nondiscretionary receipt window for ballots timely cast by Election Day would effectively federalize detailed ballot-handling rules from the word “day” in 2 U.S.C. § 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1 without a clear statement. As Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan emphasize, the more minimalist and text-faithful reading is that Congress fixed when voters must make their choice, not when election officials must complete receipt and processing, so long as no one can cast a ballot after Election Day. I would therefore keep the holding narrow: States may not permit voting after Election Day, but may count ballots state law deems timely cast by that day under a definite, bounded receipt deadline.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that §§ 1 and 7 regulate only the voter’s act of choosing, treating post–Election Day receipt as “ministerial.” But Mississippi makes receipt after Election Day a substantive condition of validity—until the ballot is received, it is not legally countable—so the federally prescribed “day for the election” does not close the class of permissible votes on that day, contrary to the ordinary meaning of “day” and Foster v. Love’s insistence that the election be “consummated” then. Roberts’s narrow-reading/clear-statement concern is ultimately a policy-based reluctance to apply the text as written; if Congress wishes to authorize post-day receipt windows for federal elections, it can do so explicitly. Justice Alito and Justice Barrett correctly identify that the relevant legal act here is not tabulation but the State’s post-day receipt rule that determines whether a ballot enters the count at all, extending the election’s operative period beyond the uniform federal day.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is the “cast-by-Election-Day” framing: that §§ 1 and 7 regulate only when the voter chooses, leaving receipt as mere administration. But Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett correctly note that Mississippi makes timely receipt a substantive condition of a ballot’s legal validity, so the universe of potentially countable votes remains contingent on post–Election Day events—precisely what Foster v. Love’s “consummated” language, read in context of a uniform federal day, is best understood to forbid. Treating receipt as ministerial (as Justice Gorsuch suggests) collapses the distinction between tabulation—which may occur after Election Day—and legal eligibility to be counted, which Mississippi itself pegs to a post-day fact. The practical consequences reinforce the textual reading: Congress’s uniform-day command aims to prevent post-day uncertainty and dispute incentives, and absent an explicit congressional carveout for mail delays, we should not infer one.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that, because Mississippi makes timely receipt a condition of countability, the “set” of valid votes is not fixed until after Election Day and thus the election is not “consummated” that day under Foster. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that Foster addressed a fundamentally different conflict—state law making the federal choice final before the federal day—and it does not clearly convert downstream mechanics of handling absentee ballots into “voting” for purposes of 2 U.S.C. § 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1. Those statutes speak in general terms about a uniform day for the electorate’s choice; they do not clearly impose a federal receipt-in-hand deadline that would predictably disenfranchise voters who timely cast ballots yet are subject to mail delays. Under a pragmatic, access-to-justice lens, absent unmistakable congressional direction, I would not read “day” and Foster’s “consummated” language to preempt a fixed, nondiscretionary, modest receipt window for ballots cast by Election Day.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that Mississippi makes receipt a condition of validity, so the pool of countable ballots remains contingent after Election Day, arguably conflicting with Foster’s “consummated” language. But Foster addressed a Louisiana scheme that made the decisive legal choice occur before the federally fixed day; extending its dictum to bar a fixed, nondiscretionary receipt window for ballots timely cast by Election Day, as the Chief Justice emphasizes, would treat downstream custody/verification as “voting” and read detailed mail-handling requirements into 2 U.S.C. § 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1 without clear textual warrant. Under a pragmatic textualist approach, the better statutory-coherence line is to anchor the federal “day” requirement to when the voter must complete the act of choosing, while allowing bounded post-day administration that does not permit anyone to cast a ballot after that day. Justice Alito’s finality/uniformity concerns are real, but absent clearer congressional language they remain policy arguments rather than a basis for broad preemption that would unsettle widespread absentee frameworks.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett press the hardest textual point: because Mississippi makes receipt by the deadline a condition of validity, the set of countable votes is not fixed on Election Day, and Foster’s “consummated” language might be read to forbid that. But Foster’s holding addressed a state scheme that made the federal choice legally final before the federally fixed day; extending its rhetoric to require in-hand receipt by Election Day reads into 2 U.S.C. § 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1 a detailed rule about mail delivery and custodial possession that Congress did not enact. As the Chief Justice notes, the more text-faithful (and separation-of-powers respectful) reading is that Congress fixed when voters must make their choice, leaving bounded, non-discretionary post-day receipt/verification rules to the States absent a clear federal command to the contrary. I agree that receipt is not purely “clerical” under Mississippi law, but the statutes’ use of “day” still does not clearly equate the completion of election administration with “holding” the election, so I cannot accept respondents’ broad preemption theory on this text and precedent.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas press the best contrary point: under Mississippi law, receipt is a condition of validity, so the universe of countable ballots is not finally known on Election Day, and Foster v. Love’s “consummated” language could be read to forbid that. But Foster’s holding addressed a state scheme that made the federal choice legally final before the congressionally fixed day; I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that extending Foster’s dictum to routine post–Election Day receipt/verification would effectively federalize detailed ballot-handling rules from the bare word “day” in 2 U.S.C. § 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1 without a clear statement. Uniformity and finality concerns (Thomas, Alito) are serious, yet on the statutes’ text and historical absentee practice, the better reading is that Congress fixed when the voter must act, not when every administrative condition must be satisfied, so Mississippi’s short, definite receipt window for ballots cast by Election Day is not preempted.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch make the best case that §§ 1 and 7 regulate only the voter’s act of choice and leave downstream receipt/verification to state administration, warning against inferring a sweeping receipt-in-hand rule from a general “day” command. But Mississippi’s law makes post–Election Day receipt a substantive condition of validity, so the legally countable electorate is not fixed on the congressionally prescribed day; that is not mere “tabulation” but a rule about what votes exist for federal purposes. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s reliance on Foster v. Love’s “consummated” language therefore fits the textual premise: Congress selected a single day on which the federal election is legally completed, and a scheme that keeps legal efficacy contingent on later events conflicts with that uniform-day requirement even if the voter mailed earlier. The absence of an explicit federal receipt deadline cuts both ways, but under a textualist approach I cannot treat a State’s post-day validity condition as outside the “holding an election” Congress fixed to a single day.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that, because Mississippi makes receipt a condition of validity, the universe of countable ballots remains “open” after Election Day, and Foster’s “consummated” language should therefore bar counting any ballot received later. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, that argument effectively redefines the federal “day for the election” statutes as a detailed federal receipt-and-processing code, even though §§ 1 and 7 speak in general terms to when the electorate must make its choice, and Foster addressed premature legal finality before Election Day rather than bounded post-day administration of timely cast votes. Justice Alito’s uncertainty/uniformity concern identifies a real consequence, but under my procedural-fairness, consequences-aware methodology it cannot substitute for a clear congressional command to invalidate established “cast-by/postmarked-by Election Day” regimes that do not permit voting after Election Day and use a short, definite receipt window. Without unmistakable text equating post-day receipt of timely cast ballots with “holding” the election after that day, I would not impose a disenfranchising rule by inference.

John Roberts.reasoning: Congress has set a uniform day for federal elections, see 3 U.S.C. § 1 (presidential electors) and 2 U.S.C. § 7 (Members of Congress), but those statutes speak to the day on which voters must make their choice, not to the completion of subsequent administrative steps like receipt, verification, and tabulation of ballots timely cast by that day. Foster v. Love preempted Louisiana’s scheme because it made the election legally decisive before the federal Election Day, thereby nullifying the uniform-day requirement; it did not squarely address, and should not be extended on this record to invalidate, state rules that treat ballots as cast by Election Day but received shortly thereafter. Given the absence of clear statutory text foreclosing a reasonable “cast-by-Election-Day” regime and the substantial reliance interests of States in administering absentee voting, a narrow holding avoiding broad Elections Clause preemption best preserves institutional legitimacy. Our decision can be limited to holding that federal law requires that voting conclude on Election Day, while permitting States to count ballots that state law deems timely cast by that day and received within a modest, fixed post-election window.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The federal statutes set a single, uniform “day for the election” for Representatives and presidential electors. See 2 U.S.C. § 7; 3 U.S.C. § 1. Under the original public meaning of “the day for the election,” as implemented by Congress pursuant to the Elections Clause and Electors Clause, the State’s rules may regulate manner but may not extend the federal election beyond that congressionally fixed day; Mississippi’s receipt-and-counting window keeps the federal election legally open after Election Day and thus conflicts with federal law under the Supremacy Clause. This Court’s decision in Foster v. Love held that the federal Election Day is the day the election is “consummated,” and a State may not move that consummation off the uniform day; accepting ballots after Election Day impermissibly shifts consummation later. Whatever administrative convenience or policy arguments exist, they cannot override the controlling statutory text and Foster’s construction of it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes—2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1—establish a single, uniform day on which the choice for federal offices must be made nationwide, and under the Supremacy Clause a state may not extend the period for determining that choice beyond the federal date. In Foster v. Love, the Court explained that federal law requires the State’s final selection to be “consummated” on Election Day, and Mississippi’s rule counting ballots first received up to five business days later keeps the ballot box effectively open after the federally prescribed deadline. Treating ballots as “cast” on Election Day does not cure the conflict where the legally operative act for counting—receipt and acceptance by election officials—may occur afterward, undermining uniformity and inviting post–Election Day uncertainty. Practical consequences reinforce this reading: extending receipt deadlines increases the risk of disputed outcomes and diminishes public confidence, while the federal text is best understood to set Election Day as the close of voting for federal contests.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes (e.g., 2 U.S.C. § 7; 3 U.S.C. § 1) set a uniform day for appointing electors and electing Representatives, but they do not clearly speak to when a State may receive and count absentee ballots that were timely cast by Election Day; absent a clear conflict, preemption should not be presumed in an area of core state election administration under the Elections and Electors Clauses. Foster v. Love is best read to forbid a State from making the decisive act of choosing federal officers occur before or after the federal day (as in Louisiana’s pre–Election Day “final selection”), not to bar routine post–Election Day tabulation or receipt of ballots mailed and cast by Election Day. Treating timely-cast absentee ballots as valid even if received shortly after Election Day advances access to the franchise for voters facing mail delays, disability, or work constraints, and avoids disenfranchisement based on administrative timing rather than voter choice, consistent with the equitable concerns reflected in RNC v. DNC (2020) about real-world burdens on voters. Because Mississippi’s rule does not open voting after Election Day and instead completes ministerial processing of votes cast by that day, it should not be held preempted without a clearer congressional command.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes (e.g., 3 U.S.C. § 1; 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7) set a uniform day for holding federal elections, but they do not expressly require that state officials receive and tabulate every valid ballot by that date; Mississippi’s law instead fixes the voter’s act of choosing by requiring absentee ballots be timely cast by Election Day, with limited administrative receipt afterward. Foster v. Love invalidated Louisiana’s regime because the State legally completed the “final selection” before the federal day, creating a different Election Day—not because all post-day counting is categorically forbidden—so reading Foster to preempt modest post–Election Day receipt of timely-cast ballots stretches its rationale. Given the Elections Clause’s allocation of primary procedural authority to the States subject to clear congressional override, and the absence of unambiguous statutory text barring States from counting ballots cast by Election Day but received shortly after, I would not find preemption; workability and statutory coherence also cut against a rule that would unsettle widespread, long-standing state absentee practices without clearer congressional instruction. This narrower reading still preserves Congress’s anti-fraud, uniformity interests by keeping the decisive act (casting a ballot) tied to Election Day while allowing routine administrative processing.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes set “the day for the election” (3 U.S.C. § 1; 2 U.S.C. § 7), but their plain meaning fixes the time by which voters must make their choice—not the date by which state officials must finish receiving and processing every ballot, especially where the voter’s act of choosing is completed by Election Day. Foster v. Love held Louisiana’s scheme unlawful because it “consummated” the election before the federally prescribed day by making a final selection in October, leaving nothing to be decided on Election Day; Mississippi’s rule, by contrast, does not move the decisive voter act earlier and instead counts only ballots timely cast by Election Day. Reading “Election Day” to forbid any post-day receipt of timely cast ballots would imply Congress silently regulated detailed ballot-handling mechanics and would risk displacing long-settled state practices without clear textual command, a result this Court should not presume in an area where the Elections/Electors Clauses leave primary administration to the States absent clear congressional direction. Where ambiguity persists in a preemption claim grounded in criminalized election regulations and federalism-sensitive timing provisions, the narrower construction avoiding unnecessary displacement of state law is preferable.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes, 2 U.S.C. § 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1, were enacted to ensure a uniform day for the act of electing federal officers, not to dictate the mechanics of ballot receipt and tabulation so long as the voter’s choice is made by that day. Mississippi’s rule treats absentee ballots as timely only if cast by Election Day, with the State merely completing the ministerial tasks of receipt and counting afterward, which does not create a second, non-uniform “day for choosing” federal officials. Foster v. Love is distinguishable because Louisiana’s scheme allowed the election to be decided before the federally prescribed day, whereas here the electorate’s choice is fixed by ballots cast on Election Day and later processing does not extend voting beyond that day. Given history, longstanding absentee-voting practice, and practical workability (avoiding disenfranchisement from mail delays), I would not read the federal statutes to preempt Mississippi absent clearer congressional direction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1) set a single, uniform day for the “election” of Representatives, Senators, and presidential electors, and under the ordinary meaning reflected in Foster v. Love, “the election” refers to the combined actions of voters and officials meant to make a final, conclusive selection. Mississippi’s rule requiring only that an absentee ballot be postmarked by Election Day, while permitting receipt and counting up to five business days later, keeps the legally effective act of voting open after the federally prescribed day and thus extends the period in which federal offices may be chosen. Under the Supremacy Clause, that conflict triggers preemption, because Congress exercised its Elections Clause authority to fix the time of federal elections and ensure a uniform Election Day, even if states retain broad power over election “Times, Places and Manner” in other respects. While administrative steps like tabulation may occur after Election Day, Foster indicates the State may not structure its law so that votes may be validly cast (in the sense of becoming countable) after that day.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes—2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1—set a uniform day for the election but do not speak to ballot-receipt deadlines, so preemption should not be inferred absent a clear conflict with state administration under the Elections Clause. Foster v. Love held only that an election may not be “consummated prior to federal election day,” 522 U.S. 67, 72 n.4 (1997), and its concern was with final determination before Election Day, not the routine post-Day administrative work of receiving and counting ballots timely cast by voters. Consistent with the practical realities of absentee voting and Congress’s broader election-administration framework (e.g., UOCAVA/HAVA), Mississippi’s rule can be understood as treating the voter’s choice as made by Election Day while allowing a short grace period to avoid disenfranchisement from mail delays, advancing procedural fairness without undermining national uniformity. Given the absence of textual direction requiring receipt by Election Day and the significant disenfranchising consequences of the contrary rule, Mississippi’s statute should not be deemed preempted.
